query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Subjecting an as‐cast refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) to a controlled liquid‐metal dealloying treatment in molten copper will induce the formation of aligned, interpenetrating Cu channels within a continuous HEA matrix. This dual-phase architecture is expected to enhance the effective heat‐transfer capability via improved conduction pathways while preserving the alloy's inherent structural integrity under plasma‐facing service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, homogeneous, single-phase refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic or near‐equiatomic multicomponent HEA) with a uniform microstructure intended for use as an intermediate material in plasma-facing reactor components.
generation.intervention: Expose the as‐cast HEA to a liquid‐metal dealloying process by immersing it in a molten Cu bath under an inert or vacuum atmosphere at an optimized temperature (e.g., around 1150–1200 °C) for an extended period (e.g., 72–96 hours) to allow selective element extraction and Cu infiltration.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be performed in a vacuum‐sealed or inert environment to prevent oxidation, at a temperature range of 1150–1200 °C for 72–96 h. Post-treatment performance should be evaluated under high-temperature conditions (e.g., upwards of 650 °C, with assessments near or above 1000 °C) and under simulated plasma irradiation loading to mimic reactor service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is designed to produce a bicontinuous microstructure: interpenetrating, aligned, nearly pure Cu channels that form conductive pathways interwoven with a structurally robust, compositionally complex HEA network. Interfacial regions may feature passivating element segregation that stabilizes the interface.
generation.mechanism: During liquid-metal dealloying, selective extraction of a more reactive element (or elements) from the HEA leads to local dissolution at specific interdendritic regions, enabling molten Cu to infiltrate and form continuous channels. Simultaneously, the remaining HEA ligaments, enriched in refractory elements with low copper solubility, retain their high-strength, thermally stable structure. The resulting microstructure thus provides enhanced heat conduction via the Cu phase while the HEA matrix supports mechanical integrity under irradiation and thermal loads.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated homogeneous HEA, the treated material is expected to exhibit substantially higher thermal conductivity—especially at high operating temperatures—due to the added conductive Cu channels. At the same time, the inherent high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance of the HEA matrix should be maintained, preserving overall structural integrity.
generation.baseline: The untreated, as-cast homogeneous refractory HEA that exhibits relatively lower thermal conductivity and whose microstructure lacks the engineered dual-phase (HEA/Cu) connectivity.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEAs that are compositionally and microstructurally amenable to controlled dealloying; the benefits are anticipated primarily at elevated temperatures (above ~650 °C) and under plasma-like irradiation conditions. The optimization of dealloying parameters (temperature, time, and melt composition) is critical, and deviations may lead to over-dealloying or detrimental phase segregation that could compromise mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thermal conductivity enhancement and the long-term stability of the Cu/HEA interpenetrating network under extended plasma irradiation and thermal cycling remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same as-cast HEA. Subject one set to the proposed liquid-metal dealloying treatment in molten Cu under the specified conditions and leave the other set untreated. Characterize both sets using SEM/TEM with EDS mapping and XRD to confirm the formation of the interpenetrating Cu channels and the integrity of the HEA ligaments. Measure their thermal conductivity across the relevant temperature range (room temperature to >1000 °C) using laser-flash analysis and evaluate mechanical properties (e.g., hardness and tensile strength) before and after simulated plasma irradiation (using ion irradiation with fluences representative of service conditions).
measurements: Microstructural analysis by SEM/TEM-EDS and XRD to verify the formation of aligned Cu channels and HEA ligaments.
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., laser flash analysis) across the relevant temperature range.
Mechanical property evaluations (nanoindentation, tensile testing) and irradiation testing (ion irradiation with subsequent surface swelling and cracking analysis).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples subjected to liquid-metal dealloying do not display both a significant increase in thermal conductivity compared to untreated HEA (particularly at high temperatures) and maintain comparable or superior mechanical properties and irradiation resistance, the hypothesis will be rejected.
